diagrams.title: Actor → Motivation → Attributes → Attribution
diagrams.subtitle: An attacker profile is built by cross-referencing three axes, never on a single indicator.

nodes.label: 8 actors
nodes.detail: Organized crime, terrorist, unskilled attacker, hacktivist, insider, accidental, competitor, nation-state actor.
nodes.exam: The complete taxonomy comes from objective §2.2: none of the 4 books provide it.

nodes.label: 12 motivations
nodes.detail: Financial gain, influence, intellectual property, notoriety, espionage, fear/chaos, extortion, curiosity, revenge, ideology, political, ethical.
nodes.exam: The same tool serves different motivations: the motive classifies the actor.

nodes.label: Internal / external
nodes.detail: An internal actor already has legitimate access; an external actor must cross the perimeter. The insider bypasses perimeter controls.
nodes.exam: An authorized user who exfiltrates data is an insider, even without sophisticated tools.

nodes.label: Resources
nodes.detail: Budget, tools, infrastructure, and persistence capability over a long campaign.
nodes.exam: An APT has sustained resources, while an unskilled attacker reuses free scripts.

nodes.label: Sophistication
nodes.detail: From off-the-shelf scripts to custom tools and zero-day exploitation, with evasion and stealthy lateral movement.
nodes.exam: Sophistication is judged by techniques, not by the number of alerts.

nodes.label: Profile
nodes.detail: Observed techniques, motivations, and attributes are cross-referenced to propose an actor category.
nodes.exam: A single IOC is never enough to attribute a campaign.

nodes.label: Attribution
nodes.detail: Probabilistic conclusion, expressed with a confidence level and reassessed with each new piece of evidence.
nodes.exam: The exam expects 'attribution with confidence', not 'certainty'.

quiz.question: Which attribute describes an actor who already has legitimate access?
